## What
Clients now judge delivery success by HTTP status alone, relabeling JSON response bodies that arrive under unexpected content-type headers before unmarshalling to prevent misread failures.

## Why
When a 2xx response carries a JSON body but a non-JSON content-type label (e.g., `text/plain`), unmarshalling fails and the client surfaces it as a transport failure, causing delivered publishes to be retried and duplicated. Status code is the source of truth; the content-type header must not shadow it.

## Changes
- **Scala client**: Added `asJson()` helper that relabels entities to `application/json` before unmarshalling; wrapped all `Unmarshal` calls in all endpoints (getTopic, getTopics, publish, getSubscriptionStats, pull, ack, modifyAckDeadline, health) with this helper
- **Scala client tests**: Added "plaintype" stub topic that returns 202 with `text/plain` content-type but valid JSON body; added test asserting it counts as delivered
- **JavaScript client tests**: Added plaintype stub endpoint and test case for 2xx with mismatched content-type
- **Python client tests**: Added `content_type` parameter to conftest `_send()` helper; added plaintype stub endpoint and test case
- **Clients README**: Documented that status decides success, not content-type label; noted each test suite has an explicit test for this scenario

Postgres stores timestamps with microsecond precision, but Java's Instant keeps nanoseconds. On Linux, `Instant.now()` populates those nanoseconds; on macOS it doesn't. - Modify window change detection to compare timestamps at storage precision instead of raw in-memory precision
- Truncate all timestamps on the way into the database, ensuring stored values are already at storage precision for lossless round trips
- Update test fixture to force sub-microsecond nanoseconds deterministically (537 nanos), making truncation behavior consistent across all platforms instead of host-dependent
- Add assertion in fixture that validates sub-microsecond nanoseconds are present
- Add new test case confirming that a flyer whose window survived a Postgres round trip is not re-selected
- Update existing test assertion to compare at storage precision

Fix ledger window comparison to use database storage precision, preventing unnecessary flyer re-fetches on Linux CI.

## Why
Postgres timestamptz stores microseconds, but Java's Instant stores nanoseconds. On Linux, Instant.now() populates the nanosecond field; macOS does not. This bug was invisible locally on macOS but failed on CI.

## Changes
- Add `ChronoUnit` import to handle microsecond precision
- Add `truncate()` utility to truncate Instant to microseconds (database storage precision)
- Pre-truncate timestamps on the way into the database so round-trip behavior is lossless and comparison exact
- Update `shouldRefetch()` to compare window timestamps at storage precision instead of in-memory precision
- Update test fixture `now` to force nanosecond population for deterministic truncation behavior across platforms
- Update window comparison assertion to use truncated precision
- Add test case "NOT re-select a flyer whose window survived a Postgres round trip" to catch the precision mismatch bug and verify the fix
